messages.author: 9ca502218c2e2949
messages.subject: strict vs weak monotonicity
parts:
Hello distancers, I am trying to run some CDS models using the Distance package in R. I am having some doubts about using monotonicity, I am not sure if I should use weak monotonicity or a strict one. Is there any rule of thumb for this? 
Regards
Antonela

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strict vs weak monotonicity
parts:
Antonela

In the absence of covariates in your detection function, the `ds()` function uses strict monotonicity as the default.  The term `strict` means checks are employed to make sure that the detection function is decreasing as a function of perpendicular distance.  That is the most plausible shape for the detection process; only under very unusual circumstances might the probability of detecting animals increase some distance away from the transect.

I suggest you keep with the default `strict` monotonicity constraint unless there is good reason to do otherwise.

messages.author: 9dce01a6123da978
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strict vs weak monotonicity
parts:
Hi Eric and all,

I may be about to state the obvious here, or possibly misinterpret (in which case please do refute and correct, Eric!). But for anyone on the list not yet familiar with the principles of distance sampling I thought it might be helpful to clarify Eric's statement that "only under very unusual circumstances might the probability of detecting animals increase some distance away from the transect". Actually, situations in which probability of detection may increase with distance from the observer are reasonably common - but most of these will involve violation of one or more of the principles of distance analysis. I can think of two principles that are likely to cause problems if not respected. One is that the position and detectability of animals is not affected by the presence of the observer (e.g. animals actively move away from the observer before being detected). The other is that variation in vegetation or other aspect of habitat that could affect either the presence of animals or their detectability should not be related to distance from the transect. There are probably other relevant assumptions of distance sampling that aren't occurring to me. In any regard, I think Eric's point that detectability of animals increasing with distance from transect is very unusual pertains to situations where the basic assumptions of distance sampling are valid. Apologies if that's all too obvious!

Best wishes,

Mark

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] strict vs weak monotonicity
parts:
Hi Mark, List,

You make some good points, but actually fear your clarification might have muddied the waters a bit, and so I'll comment on it.

It is very uncommon to have detectability not drop with distance. The only really obvious example I know of that is in the case of aerial surveys without a belly window, and then, a modal detection function might be more sensible. But dealing with that will take you away from conventional distance sampling. And if you are not in a situation where the usual assumptions hold (random transects with respect to animals, g0=1, no measurement error, observation can be approximated by a snapshot - but go to the books for a complete description), then I suspect that monotonicity constraints are the least of your worries: you need to first understand what might have gone wrong and what will be the impact, and if it is possible, or not, to salvage the data.

One should not confuse the probability of detection with the availability of animals to be detected. These two concepts, and their corresponding functions, are intertwined in conventional methods and cannot be separated out (without additional independent information), but they should not be confused. What you see in the data, e.g. a perhaps not decreasing function, will not be just detectability, in that case it is much more likely something to do with availability, most likely animal movement or transects placed not at random. 

If animals move away from your line prior to detection, then strictly, conceptually, I prefer to see that as having little to do with the detection probability. It changes the availability of animals to be detected. But conditional on the position of where the animal happens to be, it's detectability should be a function of distance and decrease with distance.

The aspect of different habitats is also a separate issue. Sure you can have say two habitats, and in one detections are easier than in the other. Then you might have an animal as 100 meters from the line in "visible" habitat being easier to see than one at 20 meters from the line in "hard" habitat. But that does not mean detection is easier at 100 meters than 20. Once averaged out across all possible animals that will be at either 20 or 100 meters, unconditional of the habitat they are in, they should be easier to see at 20. So here what you want is to include a habitat covariate, not play with monotonicity constraints.

My final advice, and to come back to the question originally asked: if you have to ask, and that's just fine of course, then you almost for sure don't want to remove the monotonicity constraints. You only do that if you fully understand what might be going on with your data and what are the consequences of doing so. In 99% of the cases, you do NOT want to do it. And the number of statistics that are made up just increased a bit...

Cheers

T
